narrative:
The model predicted a 75.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile, far below the average ranking of accepted students. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; you again sat in the bottom decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 41, your score sits noticeably above the average of 37 among accepted students and therefore gave the model some reason to expect you might pass. Unfortunately, the two weak class rankings outweighed this positive signal.

You should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the bar exam after additional preparation. Improving your class standing in future years or pursuing targeted bar-prep courses could shift future predictions in your favor.
